deep.reconstruction:
Context (from the previous page): a body carries positive and negative magnetic masses. These are the interior masses together with the equivalent surface layer taken with opposite sign. The whole complex exerts no attraction on any point of the exterior space. Gauss lists three claims. (1) The body is in equilibrium under the reaction of external masses. (2) It exerts no force on a rheophor (current-carrying conductor). (3), the harder one: it is also in equilibrium under the reaction of the rheophor. This page carries out claim (3). Notation: dm is a mass element at (x,y,z) and ∫ sums over dm. The current element ds runs from (a,b,c) to (a+da,b+db,c+dc), with current intensity 1, and S sums over ds.

(i) Equilibrium conditions for a free rigid body. The total force and the total torque vanish:
∫X dm = ∫Y dm = ∫Z dm = 0, ∫(zY−yZ)dm = ∫(xZ−zX)dm = ∫(yX−xY)dm = 0.
The '=' written after the list is struck out; '=0' is clearly intended.

(ii) Field of the current at dm (Biot–Savart). Put r² = (x−a)²+(y−b)²+(z−c)². A small sketch fixes the axes: X 'links vorn', Y 'vorn rechts', Z 'oben'. Then
X = S[(y−b)dc − (z−c)db]/r³,
Y = S[(z−c)da − (x−a)dc]/r³,
Z = S[(x−a)db − (y−b)da]/r³.
In vector form, F/dm = S (R × ds)/r³ with R = (x−a, y−b, z−c), i.e. Biot–Savart up to an overall sign convention. Gauss first wrote y, z in the X-line and corrected them above to y−b, z−c. The Y and Z lines still show the uncorrected x, y, z; the same correction is evidently intended (my completion).

(iii) Total force. Interchange ∫ and S:
∫X dm = S dc·∫(y−b)/r³ dm − S db·∫(z−c)/r³ dm.
The inner integrals ∫(x−a)/r³ dm etc. are, up to sign, the components of the attraction of the mass complex at the point (a,b,c) of the conductor. That point lies outside the body, so by hypothesis these integrals vanish and ∫X dm = 0. Likewise ∫Y dm = ∫Z dm = 0. These are the first three conditions.

(iv) Torque about the z-axis. Substituting gives
yX − xY = {[(y−b)y + (x−a)x]dc − (z−c)x da − (z−c)y db}/r³.
A pencil note reads 'what stands under the integral sign is transformed thus'. Adding and subtracting (z−c)z dc:
= {[(x−a)x+(y−b)y+(z−c)z]dc − (z−c)(x da+y db+z dc)}/r³.
Write x = (x−a)+a etc. Then (x−a)x+(y−b)y+(z−c)z = r² + a(x−a)+b(y−b)+c(z−c). Also split
−(z−c)(x da+y db+z dc) = −z[(x−a)da+(y−b)db+(z−c)dc] − z(a da+b db+c dc) + c(x da+y db+z dc).
This yields the four lines
∫(yX−xY)dm = ∫S[(r²+a(x−a)+b(y−b)+c(z−c))/r³]dc dm
− ∫S z[(x−a)da+(y−b)db+(z−c)dc]/r³ dm
− ∫S z(a da+b db+c dc)/r³ dm
+ ∫S c(x da+y db+z dc)/r³ dm.
The last two lines are regrouped (bracket at right) as
−∫S (z−c)(a da+b db+c dc)/r³ dm + ∫S c[(x−a)da+(y−b)db+(z−c)dc]/r³ dm.
The purpose is to make every factor except the explicit z one of the potential-type integrals. Gauss started '= ∫S dm/r·dc', struck it out, and introduced notation instead:
V = ∫dm/r, ξ = ∫(x−a)/r³ dm, and similarly η, ζ.
These are the potential and the field components of the mass complex at the current point (a,b,c).

(v) Continuation on the next page. The result is
∫(yX−xY)dm = S V dc + S(ξa+ηb+ζc)dc − Sζ(a da+b db+c dc) + S c(ξ da+η db+ζ dc) − ∫z S d(1/r).
The final term uses [(x−a)da+(y−b)db+(z−c)dc]/r³ = d(1/r), the differential of 1/r along the conductor. It vanishes for a closed (or endless) current. The other terms vanish because V = ξ = η = ζ = 0 at all external points, which is the hypothesis. Hence the torque vanishes, and by symmetry the other two torques also vanish. On this page the derivation stops just before these definitions are applied.
errors: No mathematical error in the displayed transformations; every algebraic step checks.
Y and Z formulas are written with x, y, z instead of x−a, y−b, z−c. Only the X formula was corrected interlinearly. This is a notational slip, and the later steps use the correct differences.

Overall sign of the Biot–Savart expression (R×ds instead of ds×R) is a convention: it depends on the axis orientation sketched, current direction and sign of the magnetic fluid. It is irrelevant to the vanishing proofs.
Interchanging ∫ and S is used without comment (unproblematic for a conductor kept at positive distance from the body).
The hypothesis needed is that both the potential V and its gradient vanish at external points. That V itself vanishes (not just is constant) follows from the decay at infinity; this is implicit.
Vanishing of the term −∫ z S d(1/r) requires the current to be closed. This is not stated on this page; it appears implicitly on the next page via d(1/r)/ds.

results.what: Equilibrium conditions of a rigid body: vanishing of resultant force and of the three moments ∫(zY−yZ)dm etc.
results.modern_name: Static equilibrium conditions (sum of forces and torques zero)

results.what: Force of a current element on a magnetic mass element in the form X = S((y−b)dc−(z−c)db)/r³ etc.

A magnetic mass distribution whose external potential vanishes experiences zero resultant force from an external current. Proof by interchanging summations and recognizing the field components of the masses at the conductor.
results.modern_name: Reciprocity / action–reaction between magnet and current (field of a magnetized body with zero exterior field feels no net force)
results.usually_credited_to: Consequence of Ampère/Biot–Savart reciprocity; standard in potential theory of the 19th century

results.what: Zero resultant torque from the current, via the algebraic decomposition (x−a)x+(y−b)y+(z−c)z = r² + a(x−a)+b(y−b)+c(z−c) and splitting of −(z−c)(x da+y db+z dc). This reduces the torque to integrals of V, ξ, η, ζ along the circuit plus an exact differential d(1/r).
results.modern_name: Torque on a magnet with zero external field (angular-momentum version of magnet–current reciprocity); exact-differential argument for closed circuits

results.what: Underlying assumption: interior masses can be replaced for the exterior by a surface layer, so their difference has zero exterior attraction.
results.modern_name: Equivalent surface distribution / Gauss–Green theorem of potential theory (balayage)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful but routine verification that a magnetic mass complex with vanishing exterior field feels no net force or torque from a closed current. It is a direct application of the Biot–Savart law and Gauss's own 1840 equivalent-surface-layer theorem. The torque computation is neat but elementary algebra, and the result follows from reciprocity known at the time.

transcription_corrections: In the first torque line, the image reads '... dc − (z−c)x da − (z−c)y db' over r³, i.e. both terms with minus sign. The transcription's grouping '−((z−c)x da − (z−c)y db)' would flip the sign of the db term.

The Y and Z lines in the image show 'z da − x dc' and 'x db − y da' uncorrected. Only the X line has interlinear corrections (y−b), (z−c); the transcription is faithful but the intended reading is with differences.
'abc = c' near the top is uncertain; it is likely a fragmentary note about the coordinates a,b,c and not part of the derivation.
The '=' after ∫(yX−xY)dm in line 2 is struck through. The intended meaning is that all six expressions equal 0.
In '− dS db', the extra 'd' is struck out: read '− S db·∫(z−c)/r³ dm'.
The line 'Was hier unter dem Integralzeichen steht, wird so verwandelt' is a lighter later insertion (pencil) above the second torque line.
Second-to-last line: '= ∫S dm/r·dc' is struck out. The final line reads 'oder ∫(x−a)/r³·dm = ξ gesetzt u.c., ∫dm/r = V'.
The axis sketch reads: 'Y vorn rechts', 'Z oben', 'X links vorn'.
